first-debate-on-radio-only.summary: In this world, the voters I interviewed lean 0.8 points further toward Kennedy than the same people did in 1960 as it was. Florida, New Jersey, Virginia flip, but Kennedy still wins, 309–213–15. The closest call is Hawaii, which holds for Kennedy by 0.1 points. Nixon wins in 33 of 100 draws. Medium confidence. Strong historical evidence agrees with the interviews.
assumptions: Voters who followed the first debate judge the nominees by their words and voices alone, so appearance and manner on screen no longer shape impressions. Television audiences shrink and the debate's effect on undecided voters is muted.
howIGotThis: What changed: The first joint broadcast of the two nominees in September 1960 is carried on radio alone, so voters hear the candidates but do not see them.

What historians found (9 findings, strong evidence): No study covers a radio-only first debate. The closest evidence is the viewer-versus-listener comparison, which is thin: one Sindlinger poll with a skewed radio sample, plus a student experiment. Gallup showed a net swing of about 4 points toward Kennedy after the TV debate, and the effect on the final result is uncertain.
The numbers: the 1960 census counts and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1960 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

howIGotThis: What changed: The Democratic nominee stays silent after Martin Luther King Jr.'s October 1960 arrest and makes no sympathetic call to his wife.

What historians found (11 findings, strong evidence): Sources show Kennedy won about 68-70% of the Black vote in 1960, up roughly 7-10 points from 1956. The call to Coretta King and the pamphlet campaign are credited at the margin, but no source quantifies the effect of silence or gives turnout figures.
